title: 6 Teaching Insights I Gained through Writing a Book
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Published on the day These 6 Things came out, this post extracts six lessons about teaching from the experience of writing a book alongside a full ninth-grade load. The first is about working with a limited view of your own biggest goals: you cannot know while teaching a lesson or drafting a chapter whether it will matter, because a million other factors bear on a student's life, and Stuart treats that uncertainty as what keeps the work humble. The second argues for settling into the right work over a long period, and includes an unusual permission, that it is fine to be an okay teacher and that the savior archetype should go, because accepting it is what frees a teacher to focus on a few things and reach a manageable greatness. The third attacks neomania directly, insisting new only makes sense once you understand why what you already have is not working. The fourth is about getting over yourself daily, illustrated by three index cards above his writing desk, EQUIPPED, ENCOURAGED, UNDERSTOOD. The fifth traces how long the ideas actually took, from a quickly written first book to a thousand micro-iterations. The sixth is about risk, and the different stakes of a free blog and a book someone pays for.
points: The permission to be okay is the load-bearing idea: abandoning the savior archetype is what frees a teacher to focus on a few things and reach a manageable greatness.
Neomania is named as an active harm rather than a harmless enthusiasm, with new justified only once you understand why what you already have is not working.
The uncertainty argument is a useful corrective: you cannot know while doing the work whether it is powerful, because too many other factors bear on the outcome.
The three index cards, EQUIPPED, ENCOURAGED, UNDERSTOOD, give a concrete test for whether a piece of teaching or writing is aimed at the audience rather than the author.
The timeline is deliberately deflationary, 400,000 blog words, workshops in 25 states and a thousand micro-iterations, set against the assumption that good frameworks arrive quickly.
quotes: As a teacher, I want the courses I teach to be 1% of the reason that my students go on to lead flourishing lives.
So you can't know if you're making something powerful while you're making it, but there are still things you can do.
It's possible to be an okay teacher by just showing up and doing a few things well. And in a sense, I want more of us to be okay with being okay.
After all, neomania is making us crazier (and less effective) teachers. New only makes sense when we clearly understand why what we already have isn't working.
Great teachers don't magically come into work with this other-oriented bent — they cultivate it, day by day, through earnest, internal work.
I need to have something, a sense of the whole of teaching, that's simple enough to hold in my head but robust enough to explore for a lifetime.
Year by year, I've moved from the guy who quit to the guy who sees himself doing this for his whole career.
